lesson.menu_desc: Cost, margin and the week it all went wrong -- and the clause that says WHICH customer you mean, and the comma that changes the answer -- 31 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- The Cake Stand
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gabriel Fernandes | Lesson 4 -- The Cake Stand

listenings.text: I have had the same stall for nineteen years, and the thing nobody believes is that a good day means almost nothing. A good day is weather. What pays my rent is the forty or fifty people who come back every single week without being asked, and I could name most of them. A customer who buys because you are two pence cheaper is not a customer, because somebody else will be two pence cheaper than you next month. The traders who last are the ones who worked out early what each item actually costs them, and then stopped looking at the stall opposite.

The week I lost money was the week the sun came out, which sounds like it should be the other way round. I made forty boxes, which was ten more than I had ever made, because I thought a hot Saturday meant more people. I sold twenty-six. Cake does not keep, so the fourteen that were left were not stock, they were just gone. What I learnt was not to bake less. What I learnt was that I had picked the number before I had looked at anything, and that a number you pick before you look is a guess wearing a suit.

extra_audio.text: You add up what the ingredients and the boxes cost you. You add the overheads that you pay even in a week when you sell nothing. You count the turnover, which is everything that came in. You take the costs out of the turnover, and what is left is the margin. Only then do you know whether you broke even.

reading.rtitle: A Number You Pick Before You Look
paras: A stall at a fortnightly market looks like the simplest business in the world, and it is not. Before anything is sold, somebody has paid for flour, sugar, butter, boxes and a table. Those are the costs that appear on a receipt. The ones that do not appear are the hours, and the hours are the part almost everybody forgets to count.

The customers who come back every fortnight are the ones who decide whether a stall survives. A regular is worth more than a good day, because a good day is weather and a regular is a habit. My neighbour David, who buys two boxes every single time, has never once asked the price. That is not loyalty to the cakes. It is loyalty to somebody he has watched turn up in the rain.

The week that everything went wrong was the week the sun came out. I made forty boxes, which was ten more than I had ever made, and I sold twenty-six. Cake is perishable, so the fourteen that were left were not stock, they were a loss. The mistake was not baking too much. The mistake was that I set the number before I looked at the demand.

Since then I write down what each box costs me, and I mark up from that number and not from what the stall next to mine is charging. Somebody who undercuts you is not really your problem, because the customers who buy on price alone were never yours. What you sell to a regular is not a cake. It is the fact that you were there last time, and that you will be there next time.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from the way a fortnightly market stall actually works.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A market stall fails when the person running it bakes too much on a hot day.
What keeps a stall alive is knowing your real costs and keeping the customers who come back, not winning on price.
The cheapest stall at a market will always take the customers from the others.

items: The text says the hours are one of the costs that appear on a receipt.

David buys every time and has never asked the price.
Paragraph 2: my neighbour David, who buys two boxes every single time, has never once asked the price.
The fourteen boxes that were left over counted as stock for the next market.
